articles.title: President Trump Doxxes Senator's Cellphone in Push For Permanent Daylight Saving Time
articles.description: U.S. President Donald Trump "doxxed" a U.S. senator today, writes the Washington Sun, by posting his cell phone number "as part of a plea for his Truth Social followers to badger his Republican ally into making daylight saving time permanent." When The Washington Sun called the number minutes after Trump's post, a recording said the mailbox was full and could not receive messages... [Senator Tom] Cotton has long detested the idea of making daylight saving time permanent. In a Senate floor speech last year, Cotton said doing so would "make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans," particularly harming kids. The Senate was only able to unanimously pass the bill in 2022 because Cotton was reportedly unaware the vote was taking place, though the measure stalled out from there. The Arkansas Republican didn't back down in a post on Saturday. "Arkansans don't want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I'll always put Arkansas first," he posted on X. Trump continued his tear against Cotton soon after. "If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn't have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so," he posted on Truth. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Cheers as jailed JD Vance heckler said to have ‘just ended JD's presidential ambitions’
articles.description: Vice President JD Vance's rally ended with a Democratic candidate behind bars Friday, but the heckler quickly became a hero to countless onlookers after video of the confrontation went viral. “Thank you so much, Vice President Vance, for the gas prices!” shouted Ben Braver , a Democratic candidate for the Florida House, during a GOP rally in Florida on Friday. “Thank you for helping us win in Iran! Thank you, President Trump! Thank you so much, JD, you are such a good vice president, you pedophile protector! I’m excited for the $5,000 check, I’m so excited!” In the video, rally attendees can be seen angrily shouting down Braver as he was escorted out of the event. The video also shows Braver being forcibly thrown to the pavement by what appears to be a law enforcement officer. The Florida Times-Union reported that Braver was charged with trespassing and resisting arrest without violence. “Holy heck, this man just ended JD's presidential ambitions in 3 sentences,” reads a statement from AllChronology Media Group , an independent digital media company, published on social media. Australian academic and writer Peter Cook argued that Braver “deserves a medal” for his outburst, while others took issue with how the political candidate was treated by security. Vem Miller, a media producer who’s claimed to be a “caucus captain” for President Donald Trump — and was also arrested and charged for bringing loaded firearms to a Trump rally, though the charges were later dropped — argued that “tackling a dude for speech is never a good look.” U.S. Marine Corps veteran and advocate Carl Wheless also took issue with how Braver was treated by law enforcement. “That was straight-up bull----. The man was exercising his right to free speech. He was not resisting and was complying with law enforcement,” Wheless wrote Saturday in a social media post on X. “There was absolutely no reason that I could see to slam him to the ground and place him in handcuffs. I hope he sues whichever law enforcement agencies that officer works for, and the organizers of the event if that officer was off-duty and working as private security.” Holy heck, this man just ended JD's presidential ambitions in in 3 sentences. pic.twitter.com/xiKKThtNS5 — News to Remember (@allchronology) October 3, 2026

articles.title: Islamabad administration seeks 10-day extension of Rangers deployment ahead of PTI’s long march
articles.description: ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad administration on Saturday requested an extension of the deployment of Pakistan Rangers personnel in the federal capital from Oct 5 to Oct 15. The request came amid the PTI’s planned long march to the capital from Oct 4. Since the call was made, the administration has the been gearing up to stop the protestors from entering Islamabad, with hundreds of containers being placed. Additional personnel have also been deployed from Sindh and Punjab police. The letter, available with Dawn , from the office of the chief commissioner requested that the “provision of 3,000 personnel of Pakistan Rangers with command structure to Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) Police may be extended from Oct 5 to 15, 2026”. An earlier notification issued by the interior ministry stated that the deployment had been authorised from Sept 20 to Oct 5. According to the previous notification, the deployment had been authorised under Sections 7(b) and 10 of the Pakistan Rangers Ordinance, 1959, and Sections 4 and 5 of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, to perform functions specified under the laws, as authorised by the Islamabad chief commissioner or the provincial government. “The deployed troops may respond appropriately in self-defence to any threats or violent activities encountered in the course of their duties as per rules/regulations in vogue,” the earlier notification stated. The interior ministry separately directed that in case of attacks by disruptive and armed groups, Rangers and police would take all appropriate and necessary counter-action in self-defence and take measures to deal with any violent activity. Meanwhile, gatherings in the federal capital are also banned under the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act 2024 , which had been rushed through the National Assembly amidst the opposition’s outcry. The federal government has warned against marching towards the federal capital or blocking roads in the city, with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi cautioning PTI “not to enter a dead-end street” and hinting at a “permanent solution” to such protests.

articles.title: Indus Waters Treaty abeyance puts millions at risk, UNHRC event warns
articles.description: UNITED NATIONS: India’s decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance has raised concerns over the water security, agriculture and livelihoods of millions of people dependent on the Indus Basin, as the six-decade-old agreement faces one of its most serious challenges. The concerns were discussed on Friday, Oct 2, at a side event held in Geneva on the margins of the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council. The Council’s current session is being held from Sept 7 to Oct 7. The event, titled “Water Justice and Climate Resilience: Advancing Transboundary Cooperation in South Asia and the Middle East,” brought together legal experts, researchers, diplomats, practitioners and civil society representatives to discuss international water law, human rights, climate resilience, environmental justice and management of shared rivers. “Trans-boundary Water Challenges in South Asia” was among the principal themes, with particular attention to the Indus River system and the legal and institutional framework governing shared waters. The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA), which administers the proceedings over the IWT, has determined that the treaty remains in force despite India’s decision to place it in abeyance. India has rejected the arbitration process, while Pakistan has cited the court’s order as supporting its position that the agreement remains effective. Rashida Abbas, founder of the Hydro-Justice Student Research & Policy Fellowship and a PhD candidate at the University of Geneva, addressed the South Asian dimension of the discussion, focusing particularly on the Indus system. Abbas said rivers should not be viewed solely as matters between states because their consequences are experienced directly by people and communities. “Rivers are not experienced only by states,” Abbas said. “They are experienced by people.” She linked water governance with human rights, noting that decisions concerning rivers can affect drinking water, agriculture, livelihoods, communities and health. Abbas argued that the future management of South Asia’s shared waters should be based on law, dialogue, science, functioning institutions and justice. She also stressed that trans-boundary agreements should not become optional when relations between states deteriorate. The discussion addressed concerns about using shared water resources as instruments of political pressure. Abbas highlighted the interests of downstream communities and the need for legal frameworks to protect their water security and human rights. Other speakers placed the Indus dispute within a broader discussion of trans-boundary water challenges. Majid Hawi Alwan addressed geopolitical pressures surrounding shared water systems in arid regions, including the Gulf and wider Middle East. His contribution focused on regional approaches in which water security is treated as a shared necessity rather than an instrument of unilateral leverage. Seraina Eldada brought a mediation and diplomacy perspective, examining the institutional design of transboundary water arrangements and the role of third-party mediation and permanent mechanisms in resolving disputes. Harmayn Mujahid, a legal scholar and fellowship coordination officer, linked water insecurity with human rights concerns. The discussion considered how changing river patterns and climate-related stress can affect vulnerable communities and why questions of equity need to be considered alongside state sovereignty in international water law. Tahir Mahmood addressed the relationship between resource scarcity and security, including risks associated with water-related tensions in regions already affected by political and territorial disputes. He also discussed prevention and resilience in the context of what he described as ��hydro-terrorism.” The contributors noted that shared river systems face increasing pressure from climate change, population growth, environmental degradation and rising demand for freshwater. For Pakistan, the Indus Basin is particularly significant because its waters support agriculture, food production and millions of livelihoods. The river system has sustained human settlements in the region for thousands of years. The Geneva discussion placed the current India-Pakistan dispute within a wider question of whether institutions governing shared rivers can continue to function during periods of political tension. The PCA award represents a significant development in the legal proceedings, but it has not resolved the underlying political disagreement between India and Pakistan. The award and the separate order concerning interim measures, however, remain on the PCA’s official record. The Geneva meeting underscored the importance of maintaining established mechanisms for dialogue and dispute resolution as countries sharing vital water resources confront both political tensions and growing environmental pressures.

articles.title: Scoop: Trump's top national security aides meet secretly at Camp David on Iran, Yemen
articles.description: President Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, three U.S. officials told Axios. Why it matters: The highly unusual meeting was not announced by the Trump administration. The last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the officials said. Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine. "Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East. The White House declined to comment. Driving the news: With negotiations stalled, President Trump is considering resuming major combat operations in Iran. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said on Thursday. At the same time, Trump is being asked to join Saudi Arabia's planned offensive against the Houthis in Yemen. The Saudis are urging the president to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. Trump has been leaning against it, but U.S. officials say he could change his mind.
